food.text: At Chiripa on the shore of Lake Titicaca, farmers kept small gardens where quinoa and other plants were harvested for eating. Around 800 BCE, samples from the site's central mound were made up almost entirely of quinoa.

Carbon isotope analysis of human bones from Chavín sites showed a diet based mainly on C3 foods such as potatoes and quinoa. Maize, a C4 food, was not part of the main diet. Potato and quinoa were better adapted to the frost and irregular rainfall of the high Andes.
Nazca subsistence rested largely on agriculture. Ceramic iconography and excavated remains show a varied diet of maize, squash, sweet potato, manioc and achira, plus a small trace of fish.

At Chavín de Huántar, people could grow lowland crops such as maize and high-altitude crops such as potatoes, because the site sat at a confluence of lowland and high valleys. They were also domesticating llamas in the high areas for food and to carry heavy loads on steep slopes.

The Chiripa Montículo was a public ritual space where ancestors were revered and food was served, and possibly stored, for group events. Large quantities of quinoa seeds found there suggest the grain played an important role in the activities at this location.

Excavations at Cahuachi turned up the Three Sisters of maize, squash and beans, along with peanuts and some fish. The site is thought to have been ceremonial rather than urban, and its pottery was 30% plain utilitarian ware to 70% fine polychrome.

Cerro del Gentil in the Upper Chincha Valley, dated to about 550 to 200 BCE, hosted feasts for people across the Paracas sphere of influence. Strontium isotope testing of offerings shows that people traveled long distances to feast there.

The Moche emergence is linked to intensified production of corn, cotton, beans and squash, among other crops. This supported a regional political economy in the Moche Valley. Moche society was agriculturally based and invested heavily in a network of irrigation canals that diverted river water to crops.

Around 800 BCE, quinoa negra seeds dropped sharply in frequency compared to ordinary quinoa seeds at Chiripa. Farmers may have made formal fields, weeded, and selected seed more carefully to reduce them. This shift coincided with new ritual and political practices there.

The Nazca may have worsened the effects of destructive El Niño flooding by gradually cutting down Prosopis pallida trees to make room for maize and cotton agriculture. These trees helped prevent river and wind erosion, and their loss left irrigation systems high and dry.

Around 200 BCE, a termination ritual at Cerro del Gentil included a large feast along with large amounts of pottery, baskets and other offerings. Offerings there also included bird feathers from far northern Peru.

art.text: The Chavín culture is noted for spectacular murals and carvings at its main religious site, Chavín de Huantar. Among these works are the Raimondi Stele, the Lanzón, and the Tello Obelisk. The Chavín civilization flourished in the central Peruvian Andes from around 1000 BCE to 300 BCE.

Tiwanaku's Classic Period of artistic production and political power occurred between 375 and 700 CE. Its imperial city on the southern side of Lake Titicaca is famous for the Gate of the Sun. The gate depicts a large image of the Staff God flanked by other religious symbols that may have functioned as a calendar.

Between the 9th century BC and the 2nd century CE, the Paracas Cavernas and Paracas Necropolis cultures developed on the south coast of Peru. Paracas Cavernas made complex ceramics with religious representations, while burials from the Paracas Necropolis yielded complex textiles with sophisticated geometric patterns.

The Moche civilization flourished in northern Peru from about 100 CE to 800 CE. It is particularly noted for elaborately painted ceramics, gold work, monumental constructions called huacas, and irrigation systems.

Chavín artists made small-scale pottery that was often human in shape but given animal features such as bird feet, reptilian eyes, or feline fangs. Representations of the jaguar are a common theme in Chavín art.

The Tello Obelisk, a decorated monolithic pillar, was discovered by Peruvian archaeologist Julio C. Tello at Chavín de Huántar. Its exact date is unknown, but its style suggests around 800 BCE. The stepped cross motif known as the chakana is a prominent element of its decoration.

Between the 3rd century BCE and the 7th century CE, the Moche in Lambayeque and the Nazca in the Río Grande valley in Ica emerged. Both cultures are notable for ceramic, textile, pictorial, and sculptural productions, as well as terrace agriculture and hydraulic engineering.

The earliest artistic expressions in Peru with a high degree of intellectual and technological evolution are found at Chavín de Huántar and Cupisnique, dated between the 9th and 4th centuries BCE. They include silver and gold jewelry, ceramics, architecture, and stone sculpture with symbolic and religious meaning.

The Akapana is a large terraced platform mound with a central reservoir, built by the Tiwanaku culture near Lake Titicaca and dated to about AD 400. Its form may replicate the Andean cross, or chakana, one of the oldest symbols in the Andes.

Moche pottery is highly uniform and decorated, which led people to believe the Moche were part of a corporate state system. Many scholars now contend they were instead autonomous polities that shared a common elite culture, seen in their rich iconography and monumental architecture.

Surviving Chavín textiles from looted burials feature brown dye painted on large, seamed panels of cloth. Textiles from the burials of Karwa were ritual cult center objects and depicted explicitly feminine deities. The Chavín may have carried out the first extensive production of textiles for ritual and symbolic purposes.

war.text: The Recuay of highland Peru and the Moche state on the north coast shared borders and competed for the same water sources, so relations were probably tense. There is evidence of considerable warfare between them, and the Recuay lived in a warrior-oriented society.

The Recuay culture flourished from 200 BCE to 600 CE in highland Peru. It is associated with the earliest emergence of fortified centres and towns in the Peruvian Andes, and its fortified buildings and iconography reflect a warrior-oriented society.

In 2005, archaeologists found the mummified Lady of Cao at Huaca Cao Viejo, part of the El Brujo site near Trujillo. Her tomb, undisturbed since about 450 AD, held military artifacts including war clubs and spear throwers. It also held the remains of a garroted teenage girl, probably a servant.

Chavín de Huántar, built mainly for religion, lacked residential structures, occupational deposits, generalized weaponry and evidence of storage. Its architecture focused on temples and what lay inside them, so the site was not a fortress or a barracks.

The Paracas Textile, made between 300 BCE and 100 AD, has a three-dimensional edging of 90 detailed figures. They include warriors or lords carrying war paraphernalia, as well as women, shamans and two llamas. The mantle is now in the Brooklyn Museum.

literature.text: The Chavín culture, which flourished in the northern Andean highlands of Peru from around 900 BCE to around 250 BCE, left no written language behind. Because of this, the name the Chavín people used for themselves is unknown, and so is the language they spoke, which is probably now extinct.

Tiwanaku, a great city near Lake Titicaca that grew in the early centuries of the first millennium AD, had no written language. Its inhabitants' own name for it may therefore have been lost. The Jesuit chronicler Bernabé Cobo reported that it was once called taypiqala, an Aymara word meaning "stone in the center".

A quipu usually consists of cotton or camelid fiber cords and holds information categorized by color, order and number. Some scholars argue that far more than numbers is recorded and that quipus are a writing system. That would matter greatly, since no written record of the Inca Empire survives from before the Spanish invasion.

Some anthropologists have proposed that the lost Chavín language was a form of Proto-Quechuan. They reason that the highly regular morphology and syntax of Quechuan languages would have helped communities separated by mountain ranges understand one another. Alfredo Torero dates Proto-Quechuan to around the beginning of the first millennium BCE, when the first Chavín people had a religion.

With no written record from Tiwanaku itself, the language of its people has to be guessed. Heggarty and Beresford-Jones suggest that the Puquina language is most likely to have been the language of Tiwanaku. The site was first recorded in written history only in 1549, by the Spanish conquistador Pedro Cieza de León.

science.text: The Nazca lines are a group of geoglyphs made in the soil of the Nazca Desert in southern Peru. They were created between 500 BC and 500 AD by people who removed pebbles from the desert floor and left different-colored dirt exposed. Most lines run straight, but some form animals and plants.

The combined length of all the Nazca lines is more than 1,300 km, and the group covers an area of about 50 square kilometers. Some shapes are best seen from the air, at around 500 m, though they are also visible from surrounding foothills and other high places. Many of the shapes are made from one continuous line.

Long before quipus flourished, a possible forerunner appeared in the Andes. Quipus are record-keeping devices made from knotted cords. A plausible candidate for the earliest known precursor is a set of wrapped batons found at the site of Cerrillos, from the Late Paracas Period (c. 350 to 200 BCE).

Paul Kosok and Maria Reiche proposed that the Nazca lines worked as a kind of observatory. In their view, the lines pointed to places on the distant horizon where the sun and other celestial bodies rose or set at the solstices.

American historian Paul Kosok is credited as the first scholar to study the Nazca lines in depth. While in Peru in 1940 and 1941 to study ancient irrigation systems, he flew over the lines and realized that one was in the shape of a bird.

Paul Kosok noticed by chance how lines converged on the horizon at the winter solstice in the Southern Hemisphere. He and Maria Reiche argued that the lines acted as a kind of observatory, pointing to places on the distant horizon where the sun and other celestial bodies rose or set at the solstices.

The Moche civilization flourished in northern Peru from about 100 CE to 800 CE. Besides painted ceramics and gold work, the Moche are particularly noted for monumental constructions called huacas and for their irrigation systems.

The Nazca lines were made in two major phases: the Paracas phase, from 400 to 200 BC, and the Nazca phase, from 200 BC to 500 AD. The lines were typically cut 10 to 15 cm deep, and more than half are slightly more than 33 cm wide.

The builders of the Nazca lines removed the top layer of reddish-brown pebbles coated with ferric oxide. This revealed a yellow-grey subsoil underneath, which made the designs stand out against the desert floor.
In the 21st century, several hundred new Nazca figures have been found with the use of drones. Archaeologists believe that there are more still to be found.

Markus Reindel and Johny Cuadrado Isla made the first systematic field study of the geoglyphs. Since 1996 they have documented and excavated more than 650 sites, comparing the lines' iconography to ceramics. They believe the figurative motifs were made between 600 and 200 BC.

politics.text: The Moche civilization flourished in northern Peru from about 100 CE to 800 CE. Many scholars contend that the Moche were not politically organized as a monolithic empire or state. They were likely a group of autonomous polities that shared a common elite culture.
Ancient Peru was shaped by rising and merging societies. Many civilizations, including Kotosh, Chavín, Paracas, Lima, Nasca and Moche, developed and were absorbed by the most powerful ones.

During the Ceramic Period, various complex societies developed in the Andes. The Chavín culture lasted from 900 BCE to 200 BCE, and the Paracas culture from 800 BCE to 200 BCE. Its successor, the Nazca culture, lasted from 200 BCE to 800 CE.

Moche pottery is known for being highly uniform and decorated. This uniformity led people to believe the Moche had been part of a corporate state system. Yet the issue is debated, and many scholars see autonomous polities sharing an elite culture instead.
Moche history is broadly divided into periods. The culture emerged during Early Moche, from CE 100 to 300. It then expanded and flourished during Middle Moche, from CE 300 to 600.

Around 700 BC, Andean cultures appear to have developed systems of social organization that were the precursors of the Inca civilization. This was long before the Incas built the largest empire of pre-Columbian America.

philosophy.text: The Chavín religion was the first major religious and cultural movement in the Andes mountains. It flourished between 900 and 200 BCE. Its center was Chavín de Huántar, where the Lanzón stela was housed.

The Nazca lines were more than desert drawings. Researchers Nicola Masini and Giuseppe Orefici found geoglyphs with ceremonial motifs and others aligned to winter solstice and equinox sunsets. They believe the lines hosted events tied to the agriculture calendar and strengthened social cohesion among pilgrims who shared common ancestors and religious beliefs.

Devotees at Chavín de Huántar were led into a maze of pitch-black tunnels in the Old Temple, having been given the hallucinogenic San Pedro cactus before entering. Their disorientation, together with the drug's hallucinogenic effects, only heightened the visual and psychological impact when they eventually came face to face with the Lanzón. It was a snarling, clawed, jaguar-toothed figure whose deep-set carving of eyes, nose, lips and teeth added a feeling of ferocity.

The Raimondi Stele shows the Staff God, but flipped upside-down the image changes. The headdress reads as a row of smiling, fanged faces, and the deity's face becomes a smiling reptile. This speaks to Andean concerns with duality, and transformation is intrinsic to Chavín cosmology.

The Lanzón is associated with camay, the Andean belief that an object can be a conduit for a deity. Although it was made of terrestrial material, it was thought to house a celestial being. The people of Chavín even brought it offerings of food and ceramics.

The Staff God on the Raimondi Stele is an anthropomorphic creature with human, feline, reptilian and avian characteristics. The animals it combines are all apex predators. Their strength reflected the all-encompassing power of the Staff God, the main deity of the Chavín.

At Paracas Cavernas, shaft tombs on Cerro Colorado held multiple burials and were reused over the centuries. In some cases the heads of the deceased were taken out, apparently for rituals, and later reburied.

Cerro del Gentil in the Upper Chincha Valley hosted feasts for people across the Paracas sphere of influence. Strontium isotope tests show that people traveled long distances to attend. Around 200 BCE a termination ritual took place there, with a large feast and large amounts of pottery and baskets offered.

The Lanzón takes its name from the Spanish word for lance, but its shape more closely resembles a highland plow. Because of this, it is suspected that the deity it depicts was linked to agrarian worship.

The Paracas Textile, a finely woven mantle now in the Brooklyn Museum, has a delicate edging that suggests it was never hung. It was most likely laid out on the ground as a field for divination. Lois Martin suggests it may have been used as a calendar to track the timing of rituals.

culture.text: The Paracas people of the Ica Region of Peru, active between about 800 BCE and 100 BCE, were known for their knowledge of irrigation and water management. They also made major contributions to the textile arts. Much of what we know about their lives comes from excavations at the seaside Paracas site.

The Nazca of southern Peru built the Nazca lines, immense designs in the desert whose purpose is unknown. They also dug puquios, underground aqueducts for irrigation and domestic water, several dozen of which still function today. Both projects would have required the coordination of large groups of laborers.

The Paracas Cavernas were shaft tombs set into the top of Cerro Colorado, each holding multiple burials. Over the centuries the tombs were reused. In some cases the heads of the deceased were taken out, apparently for rituals, and later reburied.

The Paracas Textile, held by the Brooklyn Museum, is a mantle of cotton and camelid fibers measuring 62 by 148 cm. Its central web is patterned with 32 repeating rayed heads in six colors, and its edging is a procession of 90 detailed figures, including warriors or lords, women, shamans and two llamas.

Between the 8th century BCE and the 1st century CE, the Paracas Cavernas and Paracas Necropolis cultures developed. The former produced polychrome ceramics with religious representations. The latter is known for monochrome ceramics and complex, delicate textiles.

The Wari Kayan necropolis consisted of two clusters of hundreds of burials set closely together inside and around abandoned buildings on the steep north slope of Cerro Colorado. Each burial was a conical textile-wrapped bundle, most holding a seated individual facing north across the bay of Paracas. Each body was bound with cord to hold it in a seated position, then wrapped in many layers of intricate, finely woven textiles. Grave offerings beside the dead included ceramics, foodstuffs, baskets and weapons.

During the late Paracas phase, from 380 to 260 BCE, Paracas ceramics became more uniform and more people visited the huacas of the southern coast of Peru. This period also saw the growing presence of the Oculate Being, a creature that was a major part of the religious imagery.

The colors of the Paracas Textile's central web were made by the painstaking warp wrapping method, in which sections of the warp were covered with dyed camelid fleece. The plain weave over the wrapped areas created a double faced cloth whose two sides mirror each other perfectly. The design's symmetry is broken only on the long edges.
